title: CourtRank | Sebastian Sanchez
description: Case study for CourtRank, a padel club platform with a Java backend, live web product, and iOS app published on the Apple App Store.
ogDescription: A padel club platform built with Java, Spring Boot, PostgreSQL, React Native, and Next.js.
name: CourtRank
headline: A multi-platform product for turning padel club operations into real software.
summary: CourtRank started as a product idea for organizing the experience around a padel club: reservations, players, rankings, administration, and communication. It became a real platform with a live web product, an iOS app published on the Apple App Store, and Android distribution in progress.

problem.title: The problem
problem.body: A padel club is not just a court schedule. There are players, reservations, availability, user relationships, rankings, points, internal communication, and admin workflows that need to coexist without becoming operational chaos.
points: Centralize reservations and administration into a clear experience.
Connect players, clubs, and competitive activity inside the same product.
Create a technical foundation that could grow without rewriting everything after the first release.

role.title: My role
role.body: I worked across the product end to end, with a strong focus on backend and architecture, while also contributing to web, mobile, integration, deployment, debugging, and iteration.

sections.title: What I built
sections.body: I designed and implemented backend components, web and mobile clients, and product flows that support the core operation of the platform.
points: Authentication and user management.
Club management and admin workflows.
Court reservations and availability.
Player relationships and social activity.
Rankings, competitive experiences, and loyalty points.
Web and mobile clients integrated through REST APIs.

sections.title: Technical decisions
sections.body: The backend was designed so the domain would not be tangled with infrastructure or framework details. The priority was keeping clear boundaries and a foundation that could evolve.
points: Java 17 and Spring Boot for robust backend services.
PostgreSQL and Flyway for relational modeling and controlled migrations.
REST APIs as the contract between backend, web, and mobile.
Hexagonal architecture, SOLID, and dependency injection to separate domain, application, and infrastructure.
Maven, Git, and deployment workflows to support the development cycle.

sections.title: Challenges
sections.body: The main challenge was that the rules were not abstract: a reservation, club, player, or ranking has edge cases once the product starts being used for real.
points: Model reservations and availability without making the domain fragile.
Keep consistency between web clients, mobile clients, and backend services.
Design admin workflows without making the player experience feel heavy.
Move from local development to a published, usable app.

sections.title: What I learned
sections.body: CourtRank forced me to work through the full cycle, from product thinking to publication. It is the project where I have connected engineering fundamentals with practical decisions the most.
points: Data modeling matters a lot when the domain has real rules.
A clear backend reduces friction when web and mobile evolve at the same time.
Publishing an app forces thinking beyond code: distribution, stability, support, and iteration.
The best lessons appear when the product leaves the perfect development environment.

next.title: Next
next.body: Continue polishing the mobile experience, complete Android distribution, improve club workflows, and document the internal system decisions in more depth.
